notes.meaning: Bildad begins his second speech to Job. He drops all his earlier words of comfort and prepares to attack Job with harsh warnings. Bildad is angry because Job will not accept the advice of his friends.

Bildad asks Job how long he will keep talking without listening. He tells Job to be sensible so they can have a real conversation. Bildad feels that Job is just arguing instead of paying attention to the truth.

Bildad complains that Job treats his friends like dumb animals. He feels deeply insulted because Job claimed the friends lacked true wisdom. In Bildad's eyes, Job is acting proud and disrespectful toward his elders.

Bildad claims that Job is tearing himself apart with his own anger, rather than God tearing him. He asks if God should overturn the fixed order of nature just to please Job. Bildad believes the laws of God's justice are as unmovable as huge rocks and will never change for one man.

Bildad declares that the light of the wicked will surely be put out. In the Bible, light often represents life, joy, and success. Even the brightest spark of a sinner's prosperity will quickly fade away.

The light inside a wicked person's home will go dark. In ancient desert life, keeping a lamp burning at night was a sign of safety and life. Bildad means this person's household and family will face total ruin.

A strong man usually walks with bold, confident steps, but here his stride is cut short. His own clever plans turn against him and cause his downfall. He thinks he is marching toward success, but his bad choices trip him up.
The wicked man walks straight into a net with his own feet. He is trapped not by bad luck, but by his own foolish choices and bad actions. He wanders directly into danger without even realizing it.

A hidden trap snaps shut around the sinner's heel and holds him fast. A snare wraps tightly around him so he cannot run away. Bildad pictures him as completely caught, with no way to escape God's judgment.
Traps and cords lie hidden all along the wicked man's path. Wherever he walks, danger waits for him in secret. Bildad insists that punishment will find the sinner no matter which road he takes.

Terrors surround the wicked person on every side, chasing close at his heels. His guilty conscience gives him no peace and makes him run in fear. Everywhere he turns, he imagines disaster is right behind him.

Hunger and weakness drain the sinner's strength until he cannot stand. Disaster stands right beside him like a hungry beast, waiting for him to stumble. His former power vanishes when trouble arrives.

A terrible disease eats away at his skin and destroys his body. The phrase "firstborn of death" means the deadliest sickness death can produce. Bildad cruelly points to Job's painful skin sores to argue that Job must be a wicked man.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars suggest that the phrase firstborn of death refers to Namtar, an ancient Near Eastern god of pestilence.

notes.meaning: The wicked man is dragged out of the tent where he thought he was safe. He is marched away to face death itself, which Bildad calls the "king of terrors." Death is the ultimate fear for someone whose hope is only in this world.

Fire and burning sulfur rain down on the wicked man's home until it is completely ruined. This recalls how God destroyed the wicked city of Sodom with sulfur. Bildad implies that Job's ruined household suffered the very same judgment from God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: A few scholars translate the first part of this verse to mean that Lilith, a night demon from ancient folklore, comes to live in the abandoned tent.

notes.meaning: The wicked man is compared to a tree that dries up at the roots and withers in its branches. This picture shows total destruction from the bottom to the top. The roots represent the man himself, and the branches represent his children.

No one on earth will remember the wicked man once he is gone. His name disappears from public streets and open fields. In the ancient world, being entirely forgotten was considered one of the most terrible curses.
The wicked person is forced out of the light of life into the dark grave. He is driven away from human society and the world he loved. He does not go willingly, but is chased out because of his sins.
He leaves behind no children or grandchildren among his people. No survivor remains in the home where he once lived. This was a cruel attack on Job, who had recently lost all ten of his children.

People from all directions are shocked when they see or hear about this man's terrible end. Both people in the west and people in the east shudder with fear. His ruined life stands as a sobering warning to everyone.

Bildad finishes his speech by declaring that this is the final home of the wicked. He claims this terrible ruin always happens to anyone who does not know God. By saying this, he coldly labels Job as an ungodly stranger to the Lord.
